method: Implements Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing as described in Cheshire and Baker's paper: a zero byte is logically appended to the packet, the packet is cut at every zero into zero-terminated chunks, and each chunk becomes one or more code blocks. A code byte from 1 to 254 is followed by that many minus one non-zero data bytes and stands for those bytes plus one implied zero; a code byte of 255 is followed by 254 data bytes and implies no zero, so a run longer than 254 bytes is split into full blocks plus a final normal block. Encoding walks the input keeping one code byte open and closes it at a zero byte, at a full 254-byte block, or at the end of the packet. Decoding reads each code byte, copies that many minus one bytes and restores the implied zero except after the final block, where that zero is the phantom byte and is not part of the packet. Because zero is never a code byte and never appears in the data, a single 00 byte can delimit frames. The result gives the frame in 16-byte hex rows, its length, the overhead in bytes and as a percentage, and the code-block breakdown; decoding accepts hex with any whitespace, removes one trailing 00 delimiter, previews printable text and reports every block. This page follows the paper's reference listings without its optional trailing-block optimisation, so a packet ending in an exact run of 254 non-zero bytes costs one byte more than the published bound, and a packet of all zeros is the worst case at one code block per zero byte. Input is capped at 4,096 bytes; a 00 inside a frame or a code byte whose data runs past the end is refused with the byte position. No network access and no storage.
